explains: This is what you actually DO in a battle. You never move soldiers. You give a contingent a standing JOB — its charge — which it does forever without being told again; and when the job turns out to be wrong, you send a rider across a field with a new instruction that arrives late and passes through a captain who may decide he would rather not. Every order below carries four prices: a rider you no longer have, a DIFFICULTY the captain has to be talked past, a LOCK during which you cannot change your mind, and a real cost paid in wind or neatness or nerve. An order with no price is not a decision, and there are none of those here.

theThreeVoices.1_charges: The standing job. Every contingent always has one and always executes it, so the battle finishes with or without you. Set at deployment, changed by the SET_CHARGE order.
theThreeVoices.2_standingPlans: Conditional orders bound in advance — 'if horsemen come within a hundred paces, brace'. They fire instantly, with no rider and NO HEED CHECK, because the captain agreed while he was calm. See data/standing-plans.json.
theThreeVoices.3_improvised: Everything else. It rides a courier at ten metres a second — out AND back, so the rider is busy for twice the distance — unless the target can see the Crown Banner, in which case your word arrives in one second and costs no rider at all. When it lands, the captain weighs it once and the six outcomes decide what actually happens. See data/captains.json.
theThreeVoices.explains: Foresight is cheap and improvisation is dear. That is the whole shape of commanding in this game: the deepest skill is guessing this morning which crisis tonight will bring, and binding a plan for it while everyone is still calm.

howAnOrderTravels.1_issue: You name a contingent (or one unit) and an order. Free and instant.
howAnOrderTravels.2_signal: If the recipient can SEE the Crown Banner and is inside signal range, the order lands in 20 ticks — one second — and costs no rider. This is why high ground matters and why where you plant the banner is a real decision.
howAnOrderTravels.3_ride: Otherwise a rider goes at 500 mm a tick, ten metres a second. He is busy for the ride back too, so a captain ninety metres away costs you that rider for eighteen seconds. Past enemies he swings wide, a quarter longer; if the captain is already in the press it takes three more seconds to find him.
howAnOrderTravels.4_noRiderNoOrder: If every rider is out, THE ORDER SIMPLY DOES NOT GO. There is no queue. The scarcity is the game.
howAnOrderTravels.5_overTheHead: You may send a word straight to one UNIT, around its captain. It works, at full urgency, with no heed check of its own — and the captain is insulted for the rest of the day: minus 15 on every word you send him afterwards.
howAnOrderTravels.6_land: The captain computes his heed once and picks one of the six outcomes. He does not weigh it again until a new word comes, a quarter of his men are down, one of his own units breaks, or the Banner falls.

fields.courierCost: Riders spent. Zero means it is your own voice or your own horn and costs no rider.
fields.difficulty: Subtracted from the captain's heed when the order lands. High difficulty is where an unpaid wergild becomes a tactic that never happens.
fields.commitTicks: How long you cannot change your mind after it starts.
fields.windupTicks: How long before it begins to take effect at all.
fields.hedgeSubstitute: What a careful captain does instead when his heed lands in the DRAG/HEDGE band. Named here so no engine has to invent one.
fields.overreachSubstitute: What a bold captain does instead when his heed lands in the OVERREACH band.

charges.name: Hold Ground
charges.compiles: Stand on the ground you were given. Face the nearest threat. Brace if brace-capable and mounted enemies close within 120 m. Shoot anything in range. Do not follow an enemy who falls back. Recover cohesion and wind while unengaged.
charges.theCost: Tempo. Nothing bad happens and nothing good happens, and meanwhile the other fellow is choosing the moment.
charges.explains: The safest job and the right one nine times in ten for infantry. A line that keeps its shape cannot be pulled apart, and most defeats begin with somebody wandering forward.
charges.readOnField: A straight, patient line that stays a straight, patient line.

charges.name: Advance
charges.compiles: Walk to a named line on the field at ADVANCE pace, keeping formation, and engage whatever stands there. Units dress on the slowest unit of the contingent so everyone arrives together — if the captain is any good.
charges.hedgeSubstitute: Advance, but hold one unit back as his own reserve.
charges.overreachSubstitute: Attack the nearest enemy instead of stopping on the line.
charges.theCost: You arrive less well dressed than you set out — cohesion drains every step, and cohesion is your charge, your brace and your melee.
charges.explains: The bread-and-butter attacking job. Measured pace, ranks kept, everyone together. Its only price is neatness, and neatness is worth far more than it sounds.
charges.readOnField: The block moves and visibly frays at the edges.

charges.name: Attack
charges.compiles: Close with a NAMED enemy and destroy it. Run the last stretch. Cavalry charges home, fights, then wheels out to reform and charge again. Follow the target if it shifts.
charges.hedgeSubstitute: Advance to a forty-metre standoff and stop there.
charges.overreachSubstitute: All cavalry committed at once; will press a refused charge if the captain is boastful; pursues anything it repels.
charges.theCost: You have named a target, and the contingent will follow it — including out of your line and into somewhere you did not want it.
charges.explains: The aggressive job. Name your target with care: the battle really will chase it. Cavalry on Attack behaves like a piston — charge, strike, wheel out, reform — unless their captain is the kind of man who forgets the wheeling-out part.
charges.readOnField: A contingent that keeps closing no matter what else is happening.

charges.name: Support
charges.compiles: Take post on the named friend's open flank and stay there. Commit to his fight the moment he is pressed hard — wavering, flanked, or outnumbered at the front.
charges.hedgeSubstitute: Take post only, and never commit.
charges.overreachSubstitute: Commit at once, at the enemy's flank, without waiting to be needed.
charges.theCost: One contingent doing nothing until somebody else is in trouble.
charges.explains: The order that wins crises — and the one a captain with a grudge against that friend's lord may simply fail to hear. Below obedience 75, a support order toward a rival is refused outright, and if the friend then breaks, the deed 'abandoned' goes home to court and starts a feud that outlives the war.
charges.readOnField: A contingent standing just off somebody else's shoulder. Or standing there, watching, while that somebody else dies.

charges.name: Screen
charges.compiles: Keep sixty to ninety metres from the nearest enemy. Shoot. Withdraw automatically the moment anything comes within forty-five metres. Never accept a decisive contact.
charges.theCost: These men are not holding any part of the line, and everybody can see it.
charges.explains: What makes skirmishers and light horse work with no attention from you at all: they simply never take a fight they did not choose. Against heavy infantry it is close to unanswerable, because the heavy infantry tires faster than the screen does.
charges.readOnField: A unit that stays the same distance from the enemy no matter what the enemy does.

charges.name: Guard
charges.compiles: Stay within forty metres of a named friend and engage anything that threatens it. Never advance beyond the leash.
charges.theCost: A good unit tied to somebody else's shadow.
charges.explains: How you protect archers, crossbowmen, the relic and the Crown Banner. Forgetting to do it is how most players lose their archers to one troop of light horse they never saw coming.
charges.readOnField: Two units moving as one, with one of them always between the other and the enemy.

charges.name: In Reserve
charges.compiles: Stand behind the line and do nothing at all. Do not engage. Do not advance. Counts as an uncommitted reserve for everyone who can see it.
charges.theCost: A whole contingent not fighting — and the moment you spend it, the steadiness it was radiating goes away and never comes back.
charges.explains: Not wasted. Every friendly unit that can SEE an uncommitted reserve gains a little heart every tick, because men fight better knowing somebody is behind them. The arithmetic says hold; the battle usually says spend; the whole art is knowing which of the two is talking.
charges.readOnField: Fresh, still, dressed ranks behind the fighting — visible from anywhere, which is exactly the point.

charges.name: Withdraw
charges.compiles: Fall back toward our own edge of the field at six-tenths pace, faces to the enemy, formation kept. Disengage from contact where possible, taking the disengagement blow.
charges.theCost: Ground, which the Tide counts — a long withdrawal quietly bleeds the whole army's spirit.
charges.explains: A fighting retreat: slower than running away and far safer. Ground given this way is not disgrace, it is cohesion bought with distance. It is also the hardest ordinary job to get a frightened captain to accept.
charges.readOnField: The line moves backwards but keeps its face to the enemy. If it turns its back, that is not a withdrawal, that is a rout.

charges.name: March
charges.compiles: Column of route, four men wide, toward a named point. Engages nothing. Latecomers enter the field on this charge and must be given time and a new charge to shake out of it.
charges.theCost: A column has no front. Everything that hits it, hits it as a flank.
charges.explains: The shape armies move in, never the shape they fight in. On a road it is half again as fast. Reinforcements arrive like this, and buying them the eight or nine seconds they need to deploy is your problem, not theirs.
charges.readOnField: A long snake. If it is still a snake when the enemy arrives, somebody has made a serious mistake.

orders.name: Change the Standing Job
orders.theCost: Cheap, but it takes a second to take hold — and the charge is the thing you should have got right before the battle started.
orders.explains: Change what a contingent does when nobody is telling it anything. This is the order that makes the battle never wait for you: every contingent always has a job, and if you go quiet for four minutes the battle will still be fought.
orders.readOnField: A change in what a contingent does when left alone.

orders.name: Advance To
orders.hedgeSubstitute: Advance to a point forty metres short of the one named.
orders.overreachSubstitute: Advance and engage the nearest enemy on arrival.
orders.theCost: You arrive less well dressed than you set out.
orders.explains: Walk there, keeping your ranks as best you can. The cheapest order in the game and the one you will give most often.
orders.readOnField: The block moves and visibly frays at the edges.

orders.name: Hold Position
orders.theCost: Tempo. Nothing bad happens and nothing good happens.
orders.explains: Stand still, dress the ranks, get your breath. It is never wrong and it is never enough. Give it when you have nothing better and your men need to be able to fight properly in a minute rather than badly now.
orders.readOnField: The block tightens back into a rectangle. Breathing.

orders.name: Wheel
orders.theCost: A hundred and eighty thousand cohesion — and if you are already fighting, forty more difficulty AND one tick of free enemy blows at two and a half times damage.
orders.explains: Turn the whole line to face a different way without losing its shape. The order you give when somebody is coming round your side, and the question is always whether the rider arrives in time: a pike block wheels a quarter turn in eight and a half seconds, a troop of light horse in two. That race is why flanking works.
orders.readOnField: The line pivots like a gate, ragged at the outside end.

orders.name: Fall Back
orders.theCost: Backing out of a melee gives the enemy one tick of blows at two and a half times damage. And it is HARD: difficulty 85 while in contact, which is more than many captains will accept.
orders.explains: Step backwards facing the enemy, in order, not running. One of the three most important orders in the game, because it is how spearmen escape the press before the press kills them, and how you save a wing that is losing. It is also the order most likely to be refused, because you are asking frightened men in contact to do something delicate. Whether you CAN give it was decided at court, months ago, when you decided how these men felt about you.
orders.readOnField: The line moves backwards but keeps its face to the enemy.

orders.name: Set and Brace
orders.theCost: You cannot move. At all. You cannot chase, you cannot dodge, and if the horsemen never come you are a very well-organised target standing still under a war bow.
orders.explains: Butt of the spear in the earth, point level, shields locked. THE defence against cavalry — and it is not a bonus. It is a refusal field, twelve metres deep for pikes and seven for spears, that takes the speed out of a charge before it arrives; and because shock is the SQUARE of the speed left at contact, taking most of the speed away takes almost all of the damage away. Two traps. It is FRONT ARC ONLY, so a braced block hit from the side has no refusal at all. And refusal is multiplied by your cohesion and your morale, so a shaken, ragged brace is mostly decorative.
orders.readOnField: Absolute stillness and a level hedge of points — then, if the charge comes, horses visibly slowing in the last twelve metres.

orders.name: Open Ranks
orders.theCost: Four seconds during which you are neither one thing nor the other, and afterwards you are bad at melee and nearly useless at giving or taking a shove.
orders.explains: Spread out. Arrows care about one thing above all others: how tightly packed you are. Close order takes three and a half times the arrows loose order does — and that is not a resistance stat, it is just space. The price is that a loose formation cannot push, cannot hold and cannot receive a charge, which is exactly what the enemy's cavalry commander is waiting for.
orders.readOnField: The clearest tell on the field: you can literally see the block spread out — and see the enemy horse start moving when it does.

orders.name: Close Ranks
orders.theCost: You become the best target on the field — three and a half times the arrows.
orders.explains: Shoulder to shoulder. Everything to do with pushing, holding and receiving a charge wants close order; everything to do with not being shot hates it. Half of commanding infantry is knowing which of those two things is about to happen to you.
orders.readOnField: The block visibly tightens.

orders.name: Loose at Will
orders.theCost: Arrows. A bowman has thirty-two and a crossbowman twenty-four, and when they are gone they are gone for the day.
orders.explains: Shoot at whatever is in front of you as fast as you can. Simple and wasteful: at long range against a spread-out target you may burn eight shafts to put down one man. The archer who still has arrows when the enemy line finally comes forward is the archer who wins the battle.
orders.readOnField: A steady, ragged stream of arrows.

orders.name: Hold Your Arrows
orders.theCost: Every second you hold is damage you did not do.
orders.explains: Do not shoot. You give this to save arrows for the moment the enemy is dense, close and unarmoured, which is worth about four times what shooting at him now is worth. The hardest discipline to buy and the most valuable.
orders.readOnField: Bows down, arrows nocked, nothing happening. Extremely tense to watch.

orders.name: Aimed Volley
orders.theCost: Four seconds of winding up during which you must not move, and double the arrows. If the target walks out of the beaten zone in those four seconds you have shot a field.
orders.explains: Every archer draws together and looses at one named target on a count. Sixty per cent more hits for twice the arrows. Because arrows FLY — three seconds to reach a hundred and fifty metres — you are shooting at where a unit is going to be, and against something that is moving you will usually miss. Aimed volleys are for stationary, dense, committed targets: a pike block, a shield wall that has just braced, cavalry stalled on stakes.
orders.readOnField: A pause, then every bow rising together, then one enormous arc landing all at once.

orders.name: Plant Stakes
orders.theCost: NINETY SECONDS standing in one place hammering poles into the ground while a battle happens — and the moment you move, the stakes stay behind.
orders.explains: Sharpened poles driven in at an angle, points at a horse's chest: eight hundred of refusal over nine metres, nearly as good as a pike hedge, and unlike pikemen the archers keep shooting the whole time. The single strongest defensive position in the game. Give it early, give it where you are certain the horsemen must come, and be right, because you cannot take it back.
orders.readOnField: A visible line of poles — and afterwards, cavalry stopped dead in front of archers who are still shooting.

orders.name: Charge
orders.hedgeSubstitute: Advance to a forty-metre standoff and stop.
orders.overreachSubstitute: Charge at once from wherever he stands, however far that is, and press it home even if refused (boastful captains only).
orders.theCost: EIGHT SECONDS during which you cannot change your mind, and it is loud. Enormous wind. And on impact YOUR OWN unit loses two hundred thousand cohesion and must stand twenty seconds to redress before it can do it again.
orders.explains: The most important order in the game and the easiest to get wrong, because a charge is an acceleration problem and not a button. A warhorse needs seven and a half seconds — about thirty-four metres — to reach a gallop. Ordered from twenty-five metres your knights arrive at a trot and do a sixth of the damage. Ordered from two hundred they arrive blown. The sweet spot is sixty to a hundred and twenty metres, and you have to judge it THROUGH a nine-second courier ride, which means you are guessing where the enemy will be when the rider arrives. And against braced points the captain may simply refuse — difficulty 75, because men and horses do not want to run onto spears. That refusal is the counter working, not the game being unfair.
orders.readOnField: Lances level. The last five seconds tell the whole story: still accelerating means somebody dies; slowing means the brace held.

orders.name: Envelop
orders.hedgeSubstitute: Move to the flank and take post there without going in.
orders.theCost: Forty to ninety seconds during which that contingent is not in your line. You fight shorthanded the whole time and you cannot recall them quickly — the lock is twenty seconds.
orders.explains: Send a contingent wide around the enemy's flank and into his side or back. The payoff is enormous: a flank attack is worth about four times a frontal one and a rear attack about eight, because the shields point the wrong way, fewer men can swing back, and the fear is crushing. The cost is time, and time is what the enemy is also spending. Half the battles you lose with this order, you lose in the centre while you were being clever on the right.
orders.readOnField: A contingent peeling off and travelling in a long arc. Everybody watching can do the arithmetic on whether the centre lasts.

orders.name: Feign Withdrawal
orders.theCost: Difficulty SEVENTY — the hardest order in the game. And if the captain will not do it, or the enemy simply does not bite, you now have a unit visibly running away from your own line EMITTING REAL PANIC to every friend within ninety metres.
orders.explains: Run away on purpose so the enemy chases you out of his own line, then turn and fight him strung out and disordered. When it works it is the most beautiful thing in the game. What makes it a real gamble rather than a clever trick is that the simulation does not distinguish a false rout from a true one where FEAR is concerned — and neither can your neighbours. They see men running; they lose heart. If the enemy does not bite, you have started your own collapse.
orders.readOnField: Indistinguishable from a rout, which is the point and also the danger. The tell is the moment they turn.

orders.name: Commit the Reserve
orders.theCost: It is ONCE, and here is the bite: while a reserve stands uncommitted, every friend who can see it gains a little heart every single tick. The moment you spend it, that trickle stops forever.
orders.explains: Loose the men you have been holding. Everyone who can see it takes heart at once. You are trading a permanent trickle for a single surge, and the whole art is knowing when the surge is worth more than the trickle.
orders.readOnField: The reserve moves for the first time all battle, and every man who can see it lifts his head.

orders.name: Set the Rein
orders.theCost: Almost nothing to give, and almost impossible to enforce on the wrong man.
orders.explains: Say what this contingent does when the enemy breaks. Setting it before the battle is free; changing it mid-battle costs a rider and passes through heed like anything else — and a greedy captain in a blood-fury will fail that exactly the way he fails any order he does not like. See the pursuit policies below.
orders.readOnField: Nothing, until the enemy breaks. Then everything.

orders.name: Seal a Standing Plan
orders.theCost: A whole rider NOW, spent on something that has not happened yet — and if you guessed the wrong trigger, you spent him on nothing.
orders.explains: A sealed order with a condition written on the outside: 'if horsemen come within a hundred paces, brace'. The captain weighs it when it ARRIVES — he can refuse to take the envelope — but once he has taken it, the order fires INSTANTLY when the condition is met, with no rider, no delay and no second thoughts, because he agreed to it while he was calm. This is how you are in three places at once in a game that never pauses, and it is the loophole in the politics: you cannot make a disloyal lord obey you in a crisis, but you can get him to agree to something hypothetical at the morning briefing. See data/standing-plans.json.
orders.readOnField: Nothing — until it fires, and a unit does exactly the right thing at exactly the right instant with no rider in sight.

orders.name: Exhort
orders.theCost: PERMANENT. Every use takes eighty thousand off that contingent's morale ceiling for the rest of the battle. You are borrowing courage from the last minutes to spend in this one.
orders.explains: The commander rides down the line and shouts at them. A great surge of heart at once, plus fifteen seconds of better obedience — which is often exactly what turns a refusal into an obedience at the moment it matters. You get two, plus one more for every forty points of the commander's standing at court, so this is a court number spending itself on the field. Requires line of sight from the Crown Banner: you cannot shout at men you cannot see.
orders.readOnField: A visible surge along one contingent — heads up, ranks tightening, the line stepping forward. And, later, a contingent that never recovers.

orders.name: Move the Banner
orders.theCost: While the banner moves your signal range HALVES. You go partly deaf across the whole field in order to be heard better in one part of it.
orders.explains: Move the Crown Banner. Wherever it stands, units that can see it take your orders in one second instead of nine, and every friend within a hundred metres is steadied. So the banner's position is your voice's position, and moving it is a strategic act. Put it forward and you can command the fighting line directly. Put it forward and it can be reached — and if it falls, every unit in the army loses a quarter of its will at once and every order you ever give afterwards is a courier ride.
orders.readOnField: The tallest thing on the field, moving.

orders.name: Sound the Horn
orders.theCost: Nothing at all — which is why the cost sits earlier, in the rider you spent binding the plan and the guess you made about which crisis was coming.
orders.explains: Three horn channels exist, and a horn is not an order: it is a TRIGGER you pull by hand. Any standing plan bound to that channel fires instantly, everywhere, with no rider and no heed check. This is how you make two contingents that cannot see each other act on the same heartbeat. A horn with no plan bound to it is just a noise.
orders.readOnField: One long note, and then several things happening at once in different parts of the field.

orders.name: Sound the Retreat
orders.theCost: The field, and everything standing on it, and whatever the court decides to think about a lord who walked away.
orders.explains: End the battle now, as a withdrawal rather than a rout. Units disengage in good order if they can; men already routing are simply lost. This is a legitimate and often correct choice, because the court cares far less about the field than about the ARMY. A lord who walks away with eight men in ten can fight again in three weeks. A lord who is 'still winning' with four in ten cannot. Knowing the difference is most of lordship.
orders.readOnField: Horns, and the whole line disengaging together — a very different picture from a line breaking.

pursuitPolicies.name: Hold the Rein
pursuitPolicies.explains: Do not chase. Hold the field, keep your shape, stay safe from a counter-attack — and let the enemy's lords walk home to raise another host next spring. The disciplined choice, and it costs you money, because ransoms are money. A greedy captain fails this order on purpose and the court told you in advance that he would.
pursuitPolicies.readOnField: The winning line just stands there while the enemy runs. Eerie, and correct.

pursuitPolicies.name: Pursue to the Stream
pursuitPolicies.explains: Chase them a hundred and fifty metres and come back. Some kills, some captures, and your line is together again within a minute. The compromise, and usually the right one.

pursuitPolicies.name: Ride Them Down
pursuitPolicies.explains: Chase until they are gone. Mounted pursuers kill three and a half times faster than footmen and catch twice the ransoms, and ransomed lords are money and leverage at court. But your men accumulate BLOODLUST — up to two hundred and fifty extra difficulty on every future order — and a strung-out, blown, disordered pursuit is the softest target on the field. If the enemy kept a reserve, this is how you lose a battle you had already won.
pursuitPolicies.readOnField: Your army stops being an army and becomes a hundred separate chases across the whole map.

whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.1_bandwidth: You have two to six riders — as many as your Marshal is worth — and there are always more problems than riders.
whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.2_lateness: A rider takes nine seconds to reach the far wing. Every order is an order about the FUTURE, and you are guessing.
whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.3_locks: A charge is out of your hands for eight seconds, an envelopment for twenty. You will watch a mistake happen and be unable to stop it.
whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.4_permanence: Exhort spends morale ceiling. The reserve is spent once. Arrows run out. Stakes cannot be taken up.
whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.5_refusal: The harder the order, the likelier the answer is no — and the hardest ones are exactly the ones you most need. Whether you can give them at all was decided at court, months ago.
whyTheseAreDecisionsAndNotButtons.explains: Five separate scarcities pulling at the same moment. That is what makes it a decision. Remove any one of them and most of these orders collapse into 'always do it'.
